panels.description: Pod counts come from kube-state-metrics (`kube_deployment_status_replicas_ready`) rather than the Knative autoscaler. The autoscaler is leader-elected and a departing leader keeps exporting stale values (observed: 0 pods for ~4 minutes while 4 were actually running), which produced phantom scale-to-zero dips in this panel.
panels.title: Revision Pod Counts

panels.description:
Per-endpoint success and error rate, as a percentage of requests on that path.

Both series are computed **directly from their own counters** rather than as `100 - success`. The previous version derived the error line by subtraction and wrapped it in `last_over_time(...[6h:])`, which produced a misleading result: once traffic on a path stopped, the ratio became undefined and the wrapper held the final value on screen for six hours. A short burst of 502s at 13:11-13:19 therefore appeared as a flat 100% error line long after the errors had ended.

The `or <total> * 0` term makes each series report an explicit 0% when there is traffic but none of that class, instead of dropping out. When a path has no traffic at all the series ends, which is the honest representation.

Probe filtering uses the normalised `request_path` label from the `mesh-default` Istio Telemetry (`probe` / `metadata` / `blocked` / `other`) rather than an inline path regex. The old regex listed raw paths and silently stopped matching once paths were normalised.
panels.title: HTTP/gRPC traffic health per endpoint %

panels.description:
Request rate by HTTP response code, excluding probe traffic.

Shows **traffic volume**, not a health ratio — for success/error percentages see *HTTP/gRPC traffic health per endpoint %*.

Probe filtering now relies on the normalised `request_path` label set by the `mesh-default` Istio Telemetry: `probe` (health/metrics endpoints), `metadata` (GCE metadata), `blocked` (unrecognised path rejected with >=400, mostly internet vulnerability scanners) and `other` (unrecognised path that succeeded). A sustained rise in `other` means a real endpoint is missing from the allowlist in that Telemetry resource.

Previously this panel had three overlapping targets excluding `[45]`, `[25]` and `[24]`, which together covered every response code three times and drew duplicate series under the same legend.
panels.title: Request rate by response code

panels.description:
Per-pod request concurrency as seen by the Knative autoscaler.

**All series are per pod.** The raw `kn_revision_concurrency_stable` / `_panic` metrics are fleet-wide totals, while `_target` is per pod, so plotting them together unscaled made healthy services look like they were massively over target. They are now divided by the ready pod count (`kube_deployment_status_replicas_ready`) so all three are directly comparable.

Reading it: **stable ≈ target** means the autoscaler is holding steady state. **stable > target** sustained means it is under-scaled (or has hit max-scale). **panic ≫ stable** means a sudden burst inside the panic window, which triggers aggressive scale-up.

Excess burst capacity was removed from this panel: it is a fleet-wide absolute value, not a per-pod rate, so it does not share this axis. It is shown in **Fleet Health** instead.
panels.title: Observed Concurrency (per pod)

panels.description:
Server-side response time per revision, from Istio (`istio_request_duration_milliseconds`), in **milliseconds**.

Only successful (`2xx`) responses are included, so the percentiles reflect real user-facing latency rather than being skewed by timeouts and aborted connections (`response_code=0`).

Note: Istio does not attach `request_path` to the latency histogram (only to `istio_requests_total`), so per-endpoint latency is not available here and health/metrics probe traffic cannot be excluded. Series are broken down by revision instead.

**Probe traffic is now excluded** via the normalised `request_path` label. Previously this panel filtered only on `response_code=~"2.."`, so for a service whose real requests had not yet completed it silently plotted health-check latency (~4ms) instead — visually indistinguishable from zero.

Istio records latency at request **completion**. For long-running endpoints (this service averages ~257s) the line will legitimately show no data while requests are still in flight; use **Observed Concurrency** to see in-flight work.
panels.title: Response Time (Istio, 2xx)

panels.description:
Requests currently buffered by the Knative **activator** (`kn_revision_request_concurrency`).

**Zero is the healthy steady state for most services here.** The activator only sits in the request path when the ServerlessService is in `Proxy` mode — during scale-from-zero, or when excess burst capacity goes negative. Services with `target-burst-capacity: 0` (saga, the pdfextraction fleet) run in `Serve` mode, where traffic goes ingress -> pod directly and the activator reports nothing.

So a non-zero value here is the interesting signal: it means the activator got pulled in. For `extra-large-pdfextraction` this last happened at 12:27-12:35, exactly while the deployment sat at 0 replicas.

In-flight request volume is shown by **Observed Concurrency (per pod)**, which comes from the autoscaler polling every queue-proxy and is independent of routing mode.

defaults.noValue: Activator not in the request path (Serve mode) — this is normal.

panels.title: Request Concurrency

panels.description:
Per-pod request queue depth from the queue-proxy sidecar (`kn_serving_queue_depth`).

**A flat line at 1 is not zero.** The Y axis is now pinned to 0 — previously it auto-scaled, so a series sitting constantly at 1 collapsed onto the baseline and looked like no traffic.

The gauge is only emitted while the queue is non-empty: across all 42 series in this cluster the observed values are only ever 1, 2 or 3, never 0. A gap therefore means *no queueing*, not missing data.

It also requires `containerConcurrency > 0`; with `0` (unlimited) the queue-proxy never queues and the metric is absent entirely — use **Pod Pressure (Activator)** for those services.

defaults.noValue: No queueing (gauge is only emitted while requests are queued)
